title: Which case interview framework should you use for each type of question?
description: How to pick the right framework for any case: the three families of case questions, the eleven core frameworks and which case types they fit.
hook: Use the framework that matches the job the question is asking you to do: almost every case is either a diagnosis ("why is this happening?"), a decision ("should we do this?") or an idea-generation question ("how can we do this?"), and each family has a small set of core structures. You do not need to memorise dozens of frameworks. You need to recognise the family quickly, pick the core tree, and adapt it to the client in front of you.
body:
In this guide

  • The three families of case questions
  • How to tell which family you are in
  • The core framework for each case type
  • Smaller tools to keep in your pocket
  • Hybrid cases: a sequence, not a label
  • Strong and weak answers
  • The mistakes candidates make when choosing
  • Practise with these prompts
  • Where to practise next

The three families of case questions

Every case question asks you to do one of three jobs. Work out which, and you already know the shape of a good answer.

  • Diagnose: "Why is this happening, and how do we fix it?" Break the problem into parts that add up, find the part that moved, then fix that part. Profit, cost and process cases live here.
  • Decide: "Should we do this?" Test the idea against a few yes-or-no questions, put a number on it, and end with a clear yes or no and the conditions attached. Market entry, investment, acquisition, private equity and competitive response cases live here.
  • Generate: "How can we do this?" Lay out the options in buckets that do not overlap, size the biggest, and pick the best few. Growth, launch and pricing cases live here.

How to tell which family you are in

Listen for the verb in the prompt, and for what the client will do with your answer.

FamilySignal wordsWhat your answer ends with
Diagnose"fallen", "why", "declining", "too slow", "costs have risen"The cause, sized, and the fix
Decide"should", "is it worth", "would you invest", "how should we respond"Yes or no, the number behind it, and conditions
Generate"how can", "what options", "how should we launch", "what price"Two or three prioritised options, sized

When the prompt is vague ("help the client with its strategy"), ask what decision the client is facing. The answer will put you in one family.

The core framework for each case type

Eleven trees cover most interview cases. Each link goes to a one-page explainer.

FamilyCase typeAsk first
DiagnoseProfitabilityRevenue, costs or both? Whole industry or just us?
DiagnoseCost reductionWhich costs are in scope, and what must not suffer?
DiagnoseProcess and operationsCost, speed, capacity or quality: which matters most?
DecideCompetitive responseHow big is the threat in revenue terms?
DecideMarket entryWhat is the goal, and by when?
DecideInvestment and capacityIs the demand real, and can existing capacity stretch?
DecideAcquisitionWhy does the client want to buy?
DecidePrivate equityWhat return does the fund need, over how long?
GenerateGrowthHow much growth, by when, and what is off the table?
GenerateProduct launchIs the decision to launch made, and what must it achieve?
GeneratePricingWhat is the goal: profit, share or fast adoption?

One boundary trips people up. "Should we launch this product?" is a decision, so it uses the market entry logic. "How should we launch it?" assumes the decision is made, so it uses the launch plan. Revenue drop cases use the profitability tree but spend most of their time on the revenue branch.

Smaller tools to keep in your pocket

These are not full case structures. They slot inside one branch of a bigger tree.

  • Market sizing: for "how big is the market for X?" State your approach before any maths. See buyers' side or sellers' side.
  • Cost levers along the value chain: finds specific savings inside a cost reduction case.
  • The 3Cs (company, customers, competitors): a quick starting scan for an open question.
  • Porter's five forces: judges how attractive an industry is, inside market entry and acquisition cases.
  • The 4Ps (product, price, place, promotion): the "what to offer" branch of a launch.
  • Build, partner or buy: how to get into a new market or capability.
  • Outsource or keep in-house: make-or-buy questions in cost and operations cases.
  • A risk checklist: for "what are the risks?" and for closing a recommendation. See how to talk about risks without sounding vague.

Hybrid cases: a sequence, not a label

Real cases often mix families. Take this prompt: a restaurant group can buy a struggling rival chain for $40M and wants to turn it around. Should it? It is a decision (should we buy?) that contains a diagnosis (why is the rival struggling, and can it be fixed?). Do not force it into one memorised tree. Sequence it instead.

Step 1: the deal as it stands

The rival makes $2M of operating profit a year. If similar chains sell for about 10 times operating profit, it is worth about $20M today. At $40M, the buyer is paying $20M for a turnaround it has to deliver itself. The figures are illustrative.

Step 2: diagnose the target

Now use the profitability tree on the rival. Suppose you find two fixable problems: ten loss-making sites that together lose $1.5M a year, and food costs 2 percentage points above peers on $100M of revenue, worth $2M a year.

Step 3: value the improved business

Fixed profit: $2M + $1.5M + $2M = $5.5M. At 10 times, that is $55M. Subtract about $5M of one-off costs for closures and supplier changes: $50M of value against a $40M price. The deal works, with $10M of headroom, if both fixes are delivered.

Step 4: decide

If the deal had failed at Step 1 under any plausible turnaround, a long brainstorm about menus and marketing would have been wasted time. The sequence tells you what to analyse next and when to stop.

Strong and weak answers

A weak structure is a recited list that could fit any client:

I'll look at the market, the competition, the company and the financials.

A strong structure uses a core tree but speaks the client's language:

This is really two questions: is the chain worth $40M as it stands, and if not, can we fix it enough to close the gap? I'll start with what it's worth today, then look at which sites and costs are dragging profit down.

Interviewers have heard the standard frameworks many times. What impresses them is a structure that clearly fits this case. The structuring guide shows how to adapt a core tree.

The mistakes candidates make when choosing

  1. Picking by industry instead of by question. A bank can have a profitability, entry or pricing case. The question decides the tree, not the sector.
  2. Memorising dozens of frameworks. Eleven core trees and a handful of tools are enough. Depth beats breadth.
  3. Reciting a framework's labels. "Product, price, place, promotion" says nothing about this client. Name the branches in the case's own terms.
  4. Forcing a hybrid into one tree. Sequence the questions and let the first answer decide whether you need the next.
  5. Never revising. A good structure changes when new facts arrive. Say so out loud when it does.

Practise with these prompts

For each, name the family, the core tree and your first question.

A budget airline's profits fell 30% while its passenger numbers grew.

Show the answer

Diagnose, using the profitability tree. First question: did revenue per passenger fall, or did costs rise faster than passengers? Growing volume with falling profit often points to lower fares or rising cost per seat, such as fuel or airport charges.

A rival supermarket has cut prices 10% on 500 everyday items. What should our client do?

Show the answer

Decide, using the competitive response tree. First question: how much revenue is at risk if some of our shoppers switch? Size the threat before choosing between matching, targeted responses or holding price.

A software company wants to double revenue in four years.

Show the answer

Generate, using the growth tree. First question: where does revenue come from today, by product and customer, and is anything off the table, such as acquisitions?

Should a hospital invest $30M in a new surgical wing?

Show the answer

Decide, using the investment tree. First question: is the demand real and lasting, and can existing theatres handle more patients through longer hours or better scheduling before we build?

Where to practise next

  • Drill the skill: 20 quick prompts to find the right buckets.
  • Practise against the clock: structuring drills.
